\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

This section answers the research questions in turn and then reports the follow-up experiment described
earlier. Each
subsection changes one configuration choice from the baseline and compares agreement with the human graders,
consistency across repeated gradings, and cost.

\subsection{RQ1: Reasoning}
\label{sec:rq1}

With reasoning on, a model writes out its thinking before it gives the grade. We compare the four models graded
in both modes with reasoning off and on, over the sampled answers, each graded five times in each mode
(Fig.~\ref{fig:rq1}; the supplementary material lists the values). Only Qwen3.5 reached the output limit with
reasoning on without returning a grade, in 2 to 17\% of its runs.

\begin{figure*}[!tb]
\centering
\input{figures/fig_rq1.pgf}
\caption{Reasoning off versus on, per model and dataset. (a) Agreement with the human grade (QWK)
with reasoning off (light bars) and on (hatched bars), on a 0 to 1 scale shared with Figs.~\ref{fig:rq2}
and~\ref{fig:rq3}. (b) One row per model and dataset: the change in agreement, reasoning on minus off, with its 95\% CI;
the shaded band is the $\pm0.05$ equivalence margin. Middle: how many times more output tokens reasoning
used. (c) The within-answer standard deviation across repetitions with reasoning off (open circle) and on
(filled); filled to the right means less consistent. Every sampled answer; the supplementary material lists the values.}
\label{fig:rq1}
\end{figure*}

In most combinations reasoning left agreement almost where it was (Fig.~\ref{fig:rq1}a). The change was not
significant in fifteen of the twenty model-dataset combinations, and for GLM-5.1 and GPT-5.1 on Mohler it was
demonstrably negligible: their 90\% intervals lie inside the $\pm0.05$ margin fixed in advance. On the three
public datasets all twelve changes were positive, but seven stayed below 0.05. Reasoning raised agreement
significantly in five combinations, four of them for Qwen3.5: by 0.056 QWK on Mohler (from 0.586), 0.062 on
SemEval (from 0.538, an interval that starts at +0.002), 0.221 on RIAYN (from 0.544), and 0.172 on PT-CS code
(from 0.440). The fifth is GPT-5.1 on RIAYN, by 0.230 (from 0.561). After Holm's correction for the twenty
comparisons, three remain: Qwen3.5 on Mohler and on RIAYN, and GPT-5.1 on RIAYN. Measured as mean absolute error,
reasoning lowered the error significantly in eight combinations and raised it in none.

These gains came at a high price. Reasoning multiplied the output tokens by 9 to 925: by 9 to 62 on short
answers and 109 to 211 on code for GLM-5.1, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and GPT-5.1, and by 666 to 925 for Qwen3.5. Per
thousand grades, the cost rose from \euro{}0.02 to \euro{}0.06 at the cheapest (DeepSeek-V4-Flash on Mohler) and
from \euro{}1.2 to \euro{}30 at the dearest (GPT-5.1 on RIAYN). However many tokens reasoning used, most changes
stay inside or near the $\pm0.05$ band (Fig.~\ref{fig:rq1}b).

Reasoning also made grading less consistent. The same answer, graded five times, received more varied grades
with reasoning on in 17 of the 20 combinations, significantly in 10 (Fig.~\ref{fig:rq1}c); only GPT-5.1 on RIAYN
became significantly more consistent. Grades varied even at temperature 0: with reasoning off, the open models
gave different grades across repetitions to 9 to 56\% of the answers. Longer outputs explain only part of the
extra variation (median rank correlation 0.46 between output length and the spread of grades). Consistency is also no guarantee of quality: with reasoning off, Qwen3.5 was
the most reproducible grader on four of the five sets, including PT-CS code, where it graded worst.

One failure explains where reasoning helped. On PT-CS code, Qwen3.5 with reasoning off scored 49\% of the
answers as exactly zero, against 2\% for the teachers, and the answers it scored zero had earned on average 38\%
of the marks from the teachers. We call this the \emph{zero-collapse}: answers that deserve partial credit
receive the same score as an empty answer, so the grader can no longer tell weak answers apart. We measure it as
the share of a model's grades that are exactly zero, against the human graders' share; the zeros are genuine,
parseable scores. GPT-5.1 showed a milder form, with 32\% zeros on PT-CS code and 17\% on RIAYN, and Qwen3.5
gave 16\% on RIAYN, against 2\% and 5\% for the human graders and 9 to 13\% for GLM-5.1 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash.
With reasoning off, Qwen3.5 and GPT-5.1 were also the weakest code graders: 0.544 and 0.561 QWK on RIAYN, and
0.468 and 0.584 on all the PT-CS code answers, against 0.61 to 0.73 for the other two models. All the
significant code gains of reasoning are theirs, and reasoning roughly halved Qwen3.5's zeros on the sampled
PT-CS code answers (from 47\% to 25\%). For GLM-5.1 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, which do not collapse, reasoning
changed code agreement by $-0.044$ to $+0.077$, none of it significant. No model collapsed on short answers: on
Mohler, the models' 9 to 15\% of zeros follow the stricter of the two human graders, who gave 0 or 1 of 5 points
to half or more of those answers.

Overall, reasoning bought modest gains at a high price, never making agreement or error worse but making grades
less consistent almost everywhere. Its largest gains, 0.17 to 0.23 QWK, came on code for the two models with
the zero-collapse; on short answers they were at most 0.10. Reasoning repairs a collapsing code grader and
refines a sound one a little. Whether the prompt can make that repair without reasoning is the question of the
follow-up experiment.

\subsection{RQ2: Evaluation Guidance}
\label{sec:rq2}

Evaluation guidance, the reference answer on Mohler and SemEval and the rubric on the code sets and the PT-CS short
answers, was measured on Qwen3.5, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and GPT-5.1, each with reasoning off, on all five sets
(Fig.~\ref{fig:rq2}).

\begin{figure}[!htb]
\centering
\input{figures/fig_rq2_guidance.pgf}
\caption{Agreement with the human grade (QWK) without evaluation guidance (light bars) and with
it (hatched bars), per dataset and model, on the same 0 to 1 scale as Fig.~\ref{fig:rq1}a. Guidance is the
reference answer (Mohler, SemEval) or the rubric (RIAYN, PT-CS). Reasoning off; every answer graded both
ways.}
\label{fig:rq2}
\end{figure}

Guidance raised agreement significantly in 13 of the 15 model-dataset combinations, 12 of them after Holm's
correction (all but GPT-5.1 on the PT-CS short answers). Without guidance the models agreed with the human
graders at 0.32 to 0.57 QWK. The significant gains ran from 0.095 (DeepSeek-V4-Flash on Mohler) to 0.341 (Qwen3.5
on the PT-CS short answers), and they were as large on PT-CS code (0.149 to 0.192) as on the public data. The two
exceptions were DeepSeek-V4-Flash on the PT-CS short answers (+0.118, not significant on 84 answers) and GPT-5.1
on RIAYN ($-0.004$). Guidance cost 1.2 to 1.8 times as much per grade, for the longer prompt, and did not make
grading more consistent: the within-answer standard deviation rose in 10 of the 15 combinations, by at most
0.028.

Overall, evaluation guidance is the most reliable gain in the study: it raised agreement in almost every
combination, across three model families and both domains. A trustworthy rubric or reference answer should be
added whenever one exists.

\subsection{RQ3: Scope and Decomposition}
\label{sec:rq3}

Here, we compare grading the whole exam in one call, and scoring each rubric criterion with the same rubric,
against the baseline, one question per call with a holistic score (Fig.~\ref{fig:rq3}), on Qwen3.5, DeepSeek-V4-Flash,
and GPT-5.1 with reasoning off. Scope is measured on PT-CS code, the only set of complete exams, and
decomposition on PT-CS code and RIAYN; both are scored against each answer's final grade.

\begin{figure}[!htb]
\centering
\input{figures/fig_rq3_scope_decomp.pgf}
\caption{Agreement with the human grade (QWK) for the baseline shape, one question per call with a
holistic score (light bars), and for the alternative (hatched bars): the whole exam in one call (PT-CS
code) and criterion-by-criterion scoring (RIAYN and PT-CS code), per model, on the same 0 to 1 scale as
Fig.~\ref{fig:rq1}a. Reasoning off; every answer graded both ways.}
\label{fig:rq3}
\end{figure}

On the 295 PT-CS code answers, grading the whole exam in one call lowered agreement by 0.091 QWK for Qwen3.5
(from 0.468) and by 0.137 for GPT-5.1 (from 0.584), both significant after Holm's correction, and changed it by
$-0.024$ for DeepSeek-V4-Flash, not significantly. Per question, it cost 7\% more for Qwen3.5, and 6\% and 11\%
less for DeepSeek-V4-Flash and GPT-5.1.

Scoring criterion by criterion helped only GPT-5.1 on RIAYN, by 0.153 (from 0.561), significant after
correction, and its zeros fell from 17\% to 13\%. On PT-CS code it was unchanged ($+0.002$, equivalent to zero
within the $\pm0.05$ margin). For the other two models the changes ran from $-0.072$ (DeepSeek-V4-Flash on PT-CS
code, significant after correction) to $+0.030$ (Qwen3.5 on RIAYN). Criterion scoring cost 1.3 to 3.1 times as
much per answer, because the breakdown lengthens the output.

Overall, the whole exam never helped and lowered agreement for two of the three models, while changing the cost
per question by at most 11\%. Criterion scoring helped only GPT-5.1 on RIAYN, where, like reasoning, it led a
model that gives too many zeros to credit the rubric step by step. For the models that do not collapse, it
brought nothing or a loss, at a higher cost.

\subsection{RQ4: Models and Cost}
\label{sec:cost}

The four model families differ both in how well they grade and in what they cost. Here we look again at the
eight configurations of the reasoning comparison, the four models each with reasoning off and on, now weighing
their agreement against their cost, on the sampled answers that all of them graded: Fig.~\ref{fig:rq1}a gives their agreement per dataset, and
Fig.~\ref{fig:costquality} weighs it against cost, for short answers and for code. Across the five sets the eight
configurations reach a mean QWK of 0.564 to 0.686, and the best one changes with the dataset.

\begin{figure}[!htb]
\centering
\input{figures/fig_rq4_cost.pgf}
\caption{Agreement versus cost, one point per model and reasoning mode: (a) short answers (mean QWK
over Mohler, SemEval, and the PT-CS short answers), (b) code (mean QWK over RIAYN and PT-CS code).
Agreement is computed on the sampled answers all eight configurations graded. The horizontal axis is the cost of 1000 grades in euros,
on a log scale. Points up and to the left are
better.}
\label{fig:costquality}
\end{figure}

The configuration mattered more on code: on short answers the eight configurations fall within 0.110 QWK of
each other, while on code they span 0.239. Cost separates them far more than agreement does. On short answers it
spans more than two orders of magnitude (\euro{}0.02 to \euro{}6.2 per thousand grades). With reasoning off, the
four models reach 0.611 to 0.662 QWK at \euro{}0.02 to \euro{}0.34 per thousand grades, GPT-5.1 (0.662) and
GLM-5.1 (0.661, at \euro{}0.20) agreeing best. Turning reasoning on changes agreement by $-0.037$ to $+0.073$ and
multiplies the cost by 3 to 194; only Qwen3.5's gain on Mohler survives Holm's correction. On code
(Fig.~\ref{fig:costquality}b), reasoning raised agreement by 0.196 for Qwen3.5 and 0.144 for GPT-5.1, the two
models with the zero-collapse, and changed it by $-0.007$ and $+0.017$ for DeepSeek-V4-Flash and GLM-5.1. Without
reasoning GLM-5.1 leads (0.701 at \euro{}0.80 per thousand grades); with reasoning GPT-5.1 agrees best (0.732, at
\euro{}27), and GLM-5.1 reaches 0.718 (at \euro{}5.9).

Claude Sonnet 4.6, graded with reasoning off only, was the best configuration without reasoning over all the
answers of SemEval (0.634) and of the PT-CS short answers (0.791), at about five times the cost of GLM-5.1. On
code it stayed below GLM-5.1 without reasoning, at about four times its cost: 0.676 against 0.726 on RIAYN, and
0.620 against 0.672 on PT-CS code.

Absolute agreement also depends on which human grades are the reference. Mohler's two teachers agree with each
other at QWK 0.49, while the models with reasoning off agree with their mean at 0.62 to 0.64, with the first
teacher at 0.73 to 0.75, and with the second at 0.39 to 0.41; their remaining error there is mostly a constant
offset of about 0.15 below the teachers' mean, which they track with a correlation of about 0.80. On SemEval, the
models gave the human label to 76 to 79\% of the answers, against 59\% for a grader that marks every answer
incorrect.

Overall, GLM-5.1 was the best grader without reasoning on code, at under one euro per thousand grades, and on
short answers it matched GPT-5.1 at about 60\% of its cost. Reasoning paid substantially only for the two
collapsing models on code and for Qwen3.5 on short answers. The best code configuration on average over the two
code sets, GPT-5.1 with reasoning, agreed 0.031 better than GLM-5.1 without reasoning, at 34 times the cost.

\subsection{RQ5: Conversation State}
\label{sec:rq5}

In the conversation sub-study, Qwen3.5, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and GLM-5.1 graded the 97 PT-CS exams five times
each, every answer either in its own clean conversation or in one shared conversation per exam, in the exam's own
question order and in reverse, with everything else at the baseline configuration.

Grading inside one shared conversation lowered grades slightly (Fig.~\ref{fig:conversation}a): by 0.018 of the
scale for Qwen3.5 and 0.014 for DeepSeek-V4-Flash, both significant, and by 0.008 for GLM-5.1, not significant
(95\% intervals that resample whole exams). Answer order mattered more for individual grades
(Fig.~\ref{fig:conversation}b): the same answer scored differently depending on its position, by 6 to 8\% of the
question's marks on average, 2.1 to 2.9 times the change between two gradings in the same order. The exam's own
order also scored slightly higher: by 0.015 for DeepSeek-V4-Flash and 0.014 for GLM-5.1, both significant, and by
0.010 for Qwen3.5, not significant. A shared history changed consistency across repetitions little. Because
Qwen3.5's zero-collapse can hide order effects (an answer scored zero cannot move down), the other two models are
the cleaner read. These effects fit earlier reports: LLM judges are swayed by the order of what they
compare~\cite{wang_fair_2024} and by the position of the score options in a rubric~\cite{xu_pointwise_2026}, and
a continuous grading history has been reported to pull LLM grades away from the human
ones~\cite{zhou_histories_2026}.

\begin{figure}[!htb]
\centering
\input{figures/fig5_conversation.pgf}
\caption{Conversation sub-study, per model, with 95\% confidence intervals: (a) mean grade in one shared,
accumulating conversation minus the mean grade with a clean conversation per answer; (b) answer order
within the shared conversation, as the mean absolute change per answer between the exam's own order and
the reverse (solid) and the mean signed change (hatched). Grades as a fraction of the scale; intervals
resample whole exams. The 97 PT-CS exams, every code answer, $k=5$.}
\label{fig:conversation}
\end{figure}

Overall, how the session is run matters more for individual grades than for averages. Grading each answer in a
clean conversation avoids both the pull of a shared history and the effect of position, which also makes it the
fairer choice: a student's grade should not depend on where an answer fell in the session.

\subsection{Follow-Up: Partial Credit and Prompt Engineering}
\label{sec:rq6}

%% Numbers: experiments/analysis/instruction.py (part 1, 2026-10-16) and experiments/analysis/zero_collapse.py (part 2,
%% 2026-11-05). Only the study's sets here: HARMOGEN-R is a validation dataset, so its results are reported with the
%% guide's validation (Pedro, 2026-11-05). Development comparisons use the same-batch partial-credit control
%% (zero_collapse.pilot); the five-model comparison uses the partial-credit runs of part 1 (zero_collapse.all_models).

The zero-collapse raised a practical question: can the prompt, instead of reasoning, stop a model from scoring
partially correct answers as zero? The follow-up experiment answered it in two parts (Fig.~\ref{fig:promptexp}):
it first asked for partial credit instead of strict grading, and then wrote prompts aimed at the reasons the
models gave for their zeros. All runs used reasoning off; Fig.~\ref{fig:rq6} shows the agreement and the share of
zero grades under each prompt.

%% Defined right after the paragraph that first cites it (float rule, CLAUDE.md S9).
\begin{figure*}[!tb]
\centering
\input{figures/fig_rq6_instruction.pgf}
\caption{Follow-up experiment, per model and dataset, reasoning off: the strict prompt (light bars), the
partial-credit prompt (hatched bars), and the code prompt that came out of the prompt engineering (solid bars),
which was graded on the sets with a rubric. (a) Agreement with the human grade (QWK), on the 0 to 1 scale of
Figs.~\ref{fig:rq1}--\ref{fig:rq3}. (b) Share of code grades that are exactly zero; the dashed lines mark the human
graders' share. GLM-5.1 was graded with the partial-credit prompt on code only.}
\label{fig:rq6}
\end{figure*}

On code, the partial-credit prompt raised agreement significantly, after Holm's correction, for DeepSeek-V4-Flash,
by 0.070 QWK on PT-CS code (from 0.604) and 0.064 on RIAYN (from 0.668), and for GPT-5.1, by 0.077 (from 0.584)
and 0.106 (from 0.561). The other three models changed by $-0.018$ to $+0.034$, none significantly after
correction. Qwen3.5 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash graded the strict prompt again as a control, within 0.03 QWK of their
earlier runs. The request added 53 to 60 input tokens, 5 to 9\% of the cost per grade. With it, the cheapest model,
DeepSeek-V4-Flash, matched GLM-5.1, the strongest code grader under the strict prompt (0.674 against 0.672 on PT-CS
code and 0.732 against 0.726 on RIAYN), at about a tenth of its cost. On short answers the request changed little:
every change on Mohler and SemEval lay inside the $\pm0.05$ margin (two gains on Mohler, 0.030 for GPT-5.1 and
0.013 for Qwen3.5, were significant but within it), and none was significant on the PT-CS short answers. On
SemEval, whose answers are only correct or incorrect, it raised the mean absolute error slightly, so the request
is meant for questions worth several points.

Partial credit softened the zero-collapse of GPT-5.1 but not that of Qwen3.5. GPT-5.1's zeros fell from 32\% to
20\% on PT-CS code and from 17\% to 12\% on RIAYN, and on the sampled PT-CS code answers it agreed better with
partial credit than with reasoning on (0.706 against 0.672), at about a twentieth of the cost. Qwen3.5 still
scored 46\% of the PT-CS code answers as zero. A justification written before the score halved its zeros (to
25\%), but it made the grades of both models that tried it 1.9 to 4.1 times more variable, and for
DeepSeek-V4-Flash it was unstable ($+0.042$ on RIAYN, $-0.068$ on PT-CS code).

Because partial credit left Qwen3.5's zero-collapse in place, the second part of the follow-up turned to prompt
engineering, starting from the justifications, which show why the zeros persisted. We call a zero \emph{undeserved} when the human graders had given
the answer at least 20\% of its marks, and we examined the 439 justifications behind such zeros,
counting with keywords what they mention. In about half of them (52\%), the model named something the answer did correctly and still gave no marks. The reasons given for withholding every
mark were that the answer departed from the rubric's letter, by another approach or other names (74\%), that
parts were missing (57\%), or that the code would not compile (49\%). On one answer that the teachers gave 60\%
of the marks, all five of Qwen3.5's justifications said that the student correctly checked whether a position was
free but did not iterate explicitly through two further lists that the rubric required. The models often treated each rubric item as all or nothing.

The candidate prompts, each aimed at one of these reasons (Fig.~\ref{fig:promptexp}), were compared with the
partial-credit prompt graded again at the same time, under which Qwen3.5 gave zero to 47\% of the PT-CS code
answers. In the first round, two candidates helped, in different ways. Prompt C, which has the grader state what
earns marks before the score, cut these zeros to 12\%. Prompt E, which asks it to grade as a teacher grades a
written exam, raised Qwen3.5's agreement on PT-CS code by 0.083 QWK. Prompts B and D lowered DeepSeek-V4-Flash's
agreement on PT-CS code significantly. Because C and E helped most, with the highest mean agreement, the second round joined them into the code
prompt. It cut Qwen3.5's
zeros on PT-CS code to 10\% and its undeserved zeros from 38\% to 6\%. It raised Qwen3.5's agreement by 0.094 on
RIAYN, significantly, and by 0.057 on PT-CS code, with an interval starting just below zero ($-0.003$), and
DeepSeek-V4-Flash's by 0.078 on RIAYN, also just short of significance, leaving its PT-CS code agreement
unchanged. The mean absolute error fell in all four combinations.

With all five models, the code prompt helped on code and hurt on short answers (Fig.~\ref{fig:rq6}a). On the two
code sets it raised
agreement over the partial-credit prompt in nine of the ten model-dataset comparisons, by 0.052 QWK on average,
significantly in four (Claude Sonnet 4.6 on both sets, GPT-5.1 and Qwen3.5 on RIAYN), and lowered it
significantly in none. The mean absolute error fell in all ten, the zeros fell to 2 to 13\% of the grades
(Fig.~\ref{fig:rq6}b), and the statement before the score raised the cost per grade by 23 to 73\%. Against the
strict prompt of the baseline, the code prompt raised code agreement significantly in seven of the ten comparisons,
by 0.087 to 0.218 QWK, and lowered it in none. On the PT-CS
short answers, theory questions graded with a rubric, it lowered agreement for every model, by 0.071 to 0.121,
significantly for Claude Sonnet 4.6 and for GLM-5.1 (compared there with the strict prompt), and raised the error:
the models gave almost no zeros there (0 to 3\%, against 9.5\% for the teachers), so the prompt made them too
generous.

Overall, the prompt alone removed most of the zero-collapse on code. Asking for partial credit is a near-free gain
on code for some models but left the collapse of Qwen3.5 in place, because the models often treated each rubric item as all or nothing. The code prompt, aimed at that cause, removed most of the undeserved zeros without reasoning and
raised code agreement in nine of ten comparisons, at a small fraction of what reasoning costs. Because it made
short theory answers too generous, the guide uses it for code only.
